cards.def: A frame-story collection of tales in verse and prose, told by a fictitious company of pilgrims riding to Canterbury.
A surrounding story within which other stories are told, such as a pilgrimage in which each pilgrim tells tales.
The traditional medieval division of society into the nobility who ruled and defended, the church who cared for souls, and the laborers who provided physical needs.
Writing that exposes and ridicules vice and folly as social commentary.
A medieval genre that exposes and ridicules typical examples of corruption at every level of society, estate by estate.
Saying one thing while implying another, so that apparent praise can carry criticism underneath.
A small world that stands for the whole, as a group of pilgrims can stand for all of society.
Placing contrasting things side by side so that each brings out the other's differences.
Shifting between different idioms, genres, registers or voices within one work.
A religious journey to a holy shrine.
An experienced pilgrim, traditionally one who has visited the Holy Land.
A medieval genre of bawdy and humorous narrative, usually featuring commoners as protagonists.
A courtly tale of knightly adventure and love, often with marvels such as a fairy bride.
A poem framed as the poet's dream.
The interchanges between pilgrims that connect one tale to the next.
The form of English used in Chaucer's time, between Old English and Modern English.
The everyday spoken language of a people, as opposed to learned Latin or fashionable French.
A line of five stresses in which each unstressed syllable is followed by a stressed one, x / x / x / x / x / with an optional final unstressed syllable.
Running a word's final vowel into the first vowel of the next word so the two syllables count as one.
A remission of sins drawn from the Church's "treasury of grace."
An object venerated as the remains or belonging of a saint or holy figure.
A friar granted exclusive begging rights in a certain area, his "limitacioun."
A church living, the paid position of a parish priest.
A foundation that paid a priest only to say masses for the souls of certain persons.
Nobility based on character and virtuous deeds rather than on birth or class.
Mastery or rule over another, here a wife's control over her husband, his goods and his body.
Authority drawn from books and learned (usually male) writers.
Knowledge gained from one's own lived life, which the Wife sets against bookish authority.
The tradition holding that women are by nature irrational, morally weak and dominated by material forces.
Living unmarried and sexually chaste, as monks and clerics were supposed to.
The canon-law principle that each spouse owes a sexual obligation to the other.

cards.term: Bigamy and octogamy (in the Wife's sense)
cards.def: Two or eight marriages entered one after another, not at the same time.
A short anecdote cited as proof of a moral point.
The place where the souls of sinners suffer after death to expiate their sins before entering heaven.
A spirit that lies with mortal women.
A long, elevated courtly romance about two Theban cousins, Arcite and Palamon, who rival each other for Emily.
Boccaccio's frame tale in which ten elite young narrators each tell a tale a day for ten days.
A long French dream allegory of a dreamer obsessively pursuing a rosebud, the source of many French poetic conventions.
Chaucer's longest completed poem, about two Trojans, Prince Troilus and the widow Criseyde, who fall in love during the Trojan War.
Chaucer's first major poem, a dream vision lamenting a lost beloved.
Boethius's Latin prison book on Fortune's wheel and on how God's foreknowledge fits with human free will.
St. Jerome's antifeminist attack on marriage and women, a main source of the bookish "auctoritee" the Wife argues against.

cards.term: Jankin's "book of wicked wives" (Valerie and Theofrast)
cards.def: A single volume binding together antifeminist writings, including Jerome, Tertullian, the Parables of Solomon and Ovid's Art of Love.
